records.name: Tabasco
records.current_summary: Tabasco is one of six state legislatures (with Aguascalientes, Chiapas, Durango, Querétaro and Tamaulipas) that have enacted no legal gender-recognition procedure at all — Human Rights Watch, March 2025, against a national tally of 22 of 32 states having legislated one. HRW's dedicated March 2024 report on the state, co-produced with a local inclusion centre, documented that the absence keeps trans people's identity documents permanently mismatched and exposes them to police and institutional mistreatment — document mismatch being the practical trigger for police questioning of a visible visitor. A widely circulated January 2023 claim that Tabasco added a criminal 'anti-eccentricity' provision failed the dossier's three-source verification and is not treated as a finding.

records.name: Tamaulipas
records.current_summary: Tamaulipas carries two documented deviations. Its legislature is among the six that have enacted no legal gender-recognition procedure at all (Human Rights Watch, March 2025), keeping trans people's documents permanently mismatched — the single most visitor-relevant legal fact in the country, since a mismatched document is what prompts a police check. And the country dossier names border Tamaulipas among the states where armed-group control amplifies trans-specific risk: armed groups and local police, not the penal code, decide how a gender-nonconforming person is treated, and both have documented patterns of extortion and sexual exploitation of trans women in detention.

records.name: Yucatan
records.current_summary: Better than the regional average on visibility, though the community calls the protection cosmetic: the state's sexual-diversity march in Mérida reached its 23rd edition on 7 June 2025, drawing thousands with a lesbian contingent leading for the first time, and the 2024 edition went ahead in torrential rain — no official ban and no counter-attack is reported for 2024-25. Organisers frame what LGBT people need as public policies against discrimination rather than symbolic gestures, and the local movement dates to 2003 after a police detention. The state is not among the six refusing legal gender recognition and absent from the lethality rankings.

records.name: Quebec
records.current_summary: Quebec differs legally but protectively: it runs a distinct civil-law system and its Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms expressly enumerates gender identity and gender expression, and no hostile province-specific trans law, policy or incident pattern was found. Montreal anchors a large organised community. Federal criminal law applies uniformly as elsewhere in Canada. Risk assessed at parity with - if anything marginally better than - the national picture; the difference is one of legal architecture, not of enforcement hostility.

sources.claim: Statistics Canada's release "Police-reported hate crime in Canada, 2024" (30 Mar 2026): 4,882 hate crimes reported nationally, +1% over 2023 (rate 11.9 per 100,000, -2%); incidents targeting gender identity or expression rose for a fourth consecutive year, +8% to 139 (nearly tripled, +184%, since 2020), and of known specific motivations more than half (56 of 98) targeted intersex, transgender, agender or non-binary people; sexual-orientation-motivated crimes fell 26% to 658 but remain above pre-2023 levels, with June (Pride season) running about twice the monthly average. National series - the release shows no trans-specific provincial pattern for this division.

records.name: Ontario
records.current_summary: No province-specific anti-trans law or official hostility was found; criminal law and human-rights protection are federal and uniform, and Ontario's government has not legislated on trans names, pronouns or care as two other provinces have. Police-reported hate crime across all motivations is the highest among the provinces (16.0 per 100,000 in 2024) - an all-motivations statistic, not trans-specific. Toronto and Ottawa anchor large, organised 2SLGBTQ+ communities with institutional support. Risk broadly at parity with the national picture.

records.name: Yukon
records.current_summary: No territory-specific trans statute, incident series or policing pattern was found for Yukon in the country dossier: the national criminal law, the national self-declaration gender framework and national protections apply directly. The one territory-level figure on record is lethal gendered violence: in 2021 the three territories together recorded 3.20 gender-related homicides per 100,000 women and girls, roughly triple the highest provincial rate (1.03), with rural areas running more than 2.5x urban rates — not trans-specific, and the only official territorial rate data available. Nationally, police-reported hate crimes targeting gender identity or expression rose 8% to 139 in 2024, a fourth consecutive annual increase and nearly triple the 2020 level (+184%), while Pride-season June saw roughly double the monthly average of incidents targeting sexual orientation.

sources.claim: Statistics Canada release 'Police-reported hate crime in Canada, 2024' (published 30 March 2026): police reported 4,882 hate crimes in 2024 (+1% on 2023; +169% since 2018; rate 11.9 per 100,000). Hate crimes targeting gender identity or expression rose 8% to 139 — a fourth consecutive yearly increase and +184% since 2020; incidents targeting sexual orientation fell 26% to 658, though June (2024: 113 incidents) runs more than double the ~50-incident monthly average. Police-reported hate crime rates are ~2.5x higher in large metropolitan areas (13.9 per 100,000) than in smaller towns (5.5), which bears on sparsely-populated territories where reporting infrastructure is thinner.
